notes.b: Access to education has widened across generations, so more children and adults now complete school and continue into further study. A hundred years ago many children left school at primary level, and second-level and university education were mainly for those who could pay.
points: Today every child has free primary and second-level education and a wide choice of routes after school, so schooling no longer depends on what a family can afford.

Free second-level education was announced in 1966 by the Minister for Education, Donogh O'Malley, and has been in effect since 1967. It removed the fees that had kept many children from completing school.
School attendance is compulsory from age 6 to 16, or until three years of second-level education have been completed (Education (Welfare) Act 2000).

Third-level tuition fees for eligible full-time undergraduates were abolished from 1996 (the free fees initiative), widening access to colleges and universities. A student contribution (registration charge) remains.
Grants to meet living and other costs at third level are paid by SUSI (Student Universal Support Ireland) and are based on means, so students from lower-income families receive more help.

The free pre-school programme, the Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) programme, began in 2010 and now provides two years of free pre-school before primary school, for children of the eligible age.
Post Leaving Certificate (PLC) courses, further education, apprenticeships and adult and community education give adults a second route to qualifications for work or further study.
notes.tip: Exams ask for improvements in education. Name the scheme and give its date where you can, such as free second-level education from 1967 and free undergraduate tuition from 1996, rather than writing 'education is free now'.

notes.h: Support within school and second chances
notes.b: Free fees alone do not keep every child in school. Further supports help pupils who need extra help, who are at risk of leaving early, who come from disadvantaged areas, or who want a different route.
points: Special needs assistants and resource teaching, for example, support pupils with special educational needs within mainstream classes, so these children can learn alongside their classmates.
The School Completion Programme targets students at risk of leaving school early, through extra supports such as homework and out-of-school activities, which helps them stay on to finish.
The DEIS programme (Delivering Equality of Opportunity in Schools) supports schools in disadvantaged areas, because pupils there face more barriers to staying in school.
Leaving Certificate Applied is a modular, practical programme assessed over two years, so it suits students who learn by doing, preparing students for work and adult life.

Transition Year and Youthreach offer practical, work-based and personal development learning to young people in different circumstances. Youthreach is for early school leavers, so it gives them a second chance.
The Back to Education Allowance is an income support, not a course. It helps people on certain social welfare payments to take approved courses at second or third level.

The Higher Education Access Route, HEAR, improves third-level access for socially disadvantaged students, and the Disability Access Route to Education, DARE, does the same for students with disabilities.
notes.tip: If asked for programmes that keep young people in second-level education, choose from the School Completion Programme, Leaving Certificate Applied, Youthreach and Transition Year, and give two benefits to the student of each.

notes.h: Effects of improved education on family life
notes.b: Education changes what parents can do for their children and what a family can earn. Most effects are positive, but there are costs as well.
points: Better-educated parents are better able to help with homework and to encourage children's progress and achievement.
Educational attainment affects job prospects and earnings, so better qualifications raise the family's standard of living.
Women's education has increased their financial independence and their participation in paid employment, because qualifications open up better-paid jobs.
Adult education lets parents return to work after raising children, adding a second income to the household.
As education widens choices, families tend to be smaller and people marry later, and there is less poverty across generations.
Negative effects include the cost of books, uniforms, transport and college living away from home, and exam pressure on students.
Children may leave the area for college or work.
notes.tip: A discuss question on education and family life expects effects such as help with homework, better jobs and incomes, women's independence, smaller families and adults returning to education. Add a drawback or two to lift a weaker answer.

notes.h: Social welfare: purpose and types of payment
notes.b: Social welfare is income support from the State, through the Department of Social Protection, to people who cannot earn enough: those who are unemployed, ill or disabled, retired, widowed, parenting alone, caring for others or on low pay. It is funded from taxes and PRSI (pay-related social insurance) contributions.
points: Social insurance payments (contributory) depend on PRSI contributions paid while working and on a record of those contributions. Examples are Jobseeker's Benefit, the contributory State pension and maternity benefit.

Social assistance payments (non-contributory) are means-tested, meaning they depend on an assessment of household income and savings, so they are targeted at households in need and paid from taxation.

Examples of means-tested payments are Jobseeker's Allowance, the non-contributory State pension, Supplementary Welfare Allowance, One-Parent Family Payment, Disability Allowance and Carer's Allowance.
Universal payments are paid to everyone in a category regardless of income. Child Benefit is the main example, paid for each child regardless of parental income.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the three types: social insurance depends on your PRSI record, social assistance is means-tested, and universal payments such as Child Benefit depend on neither. Short questions test whether Child Benefit is universal and whether Supplementary Welfare Allowance is means-tested, and ask you to define means test and PRSI.

notes.b: Several payments are aimed at families with children, because children are costly and parents with the main responsibility for them may have low or interrupted incomes.
points: Child Benefit is a monthly payment for each child, paid up to age 16, or up to 18 where the child is in full-time education. It is universal. It was called Children's Allowance until it was renamed.
The Working Family Payment (formerly Family Income Supplement) supports employees on low pay who have children, making work more worthwhile.
One-Parent Family Payment supports parents who have the main responsibility for children on their own.
The Back to School Clothing and Footwear Allowance is paid once a year, means-tested, to help families on low incomes meet the cost of school clothing.
Maternity, paternity and parent's benefits support workers who take leave to care for a child, so they do not lose all income while away.
Medical cards (and GP visit cards) give eligible families free GP visits and free or low-cost prescribed medicines. They depend on means or age.
Other supports are the Fuel Allowance, the Household Benefits Package and the free travel pass for older people.
notes.tip: If asked for three payments for families with children and details of one, give its name, who is eligible and how it helps. Choose from Child Benefit, Working Family Payment, the back-to-school clothing allowance and One-Parent Family Payment.

notes.b: Welfare payments give families a safety net, but they also have drawbacks and a cost. A good answer weighs both.
points: Welfare payments reduce child poverty by giving families a regular income when a parent is out of work, ill or on low pay, so children can stay in school and have more activities.
Old age pensions give older people financial independence, so they do not depend on their adult children.
Carer's payments allow a family member to care for an elderly or disabled relative at home, for example without giving up all income.
Lone-parent families can support their children because of payments such as One-Parent Family Payment, which replace part of a second income.
Conditions attached to payments, such as job-seeking and activation requirements for jobseekers, means tests and contribution records, aim to avoid long-term dependence on welfare.
Criticisms are that payments can be low relative to living costs, that people can become dependent on welfare, and that extra earnings can reduce payments, a trap called the poverty trap.
Critics argue that welfare can discourage people from taking up low-paid work, which is why work incentives form part of many schemes.
Some people feel stigma in claiming, and welfare is a cost to taxpayers because it is funded from taxes and PRSI.
notes.tip: Discuss questions on social welfare expect reduced poverty, income for the unemployed and sick, independence for older people and support for lone parents and carers, plus a drawback or two. Do not present welfare only as a benefit, because weaker answers leave out the problems and cost.

notes.h: Practical setting: schooling then and now
notes.b: Comparing who attended school a hundred years ago with today shows how education has changed within a family's own history.
points: Ask an older relative how many years they attended school, how many children were in their class and whether they stayed on after the minimum school-leaving age.
Record the same details for a present-day young person and compare the answers.
Note which supports, such as special needs assistants, the School Completion Programme and free pre-school, were not available to the older relative.

keyTerms.definition: Income support paid by the state to people who are unemployed, sick, disabled, retired or caring for others.
An assessment of household income and savings that decides whether a payment is made and how much it is.
A payment made to everyone in a category, such as every child, without a means test.
Pay-related social insurance, paid by employees and employers, which funds contributory social welfare payments.
Education after second level, provided in colleges and universities.
Education that gives adults who left school early a route to qualifications.
A school staff member who supports pupils with special educational needs in mainstream classes.
A card giving eligible people free GP visits and prescribed medicines.
An alternative admission pathway to third-level education for students from under-represented groups.

factCards.term: Three ways improved education supports family life
factCards.definition: Better parental help with learning, greater financial independence for women, and higher earning power that raises household living standards.

factCards.term: Four programmes or courses that help young people stay in education
factCards.definition: School Completion Programme, Leaving Certificate Applied, Youthreach and Transition Year.

factCards.term: Two types of social welfare payment
factCards.definition: Social insurance payments funded by PRSI contributions, and means-tested payments based on household income.

factCards.term: Three effects of welfare payments on family life
factCards.definition: They reduce child poverty, give older people financial independence, and help families cope with illness or unemployment.

questions.prompt: State two ways in which the state has improved the provision of education for children and young people in Ireland.
questions.model: Free second-level education introduced from 1967. A free pre-school year before primary school under the Early Childhood Care and Education scheme. Special needs assistants in mainstream classes. School Completion Programme for students at risk of leaving early.

questions.prompt: Explain how improvements in education and in social welfare have helped Irish families. Discuss one limitation of welfare support in your answer.
questions.model: Education: free second-level schooling and the abolition of third-level fees widened access, so more children complete school and continue into further study. Higher educational attainment raises employment prospects and earnings, which improves family living standards. Adult and second-chance education lets parents return to work, adding a second income. Support programmes such as the School Completion Programme and special needs assistants keep vulnerable pupils in school. Welfare: means-tested and universal payments give regular income to families with children, lone parents and low-paid workers; child benefit is paid per child regardless of income; medical cards give free GP visits to eligible families; old age pensions give older people independence. Limitation: payments can fail to lift a family out of poverty if they are low, and conditions such as job-seeking requirements or income thresholds can discourage some people from taking low-paid work.
